hints: Think about whether each process needs energy put in to separate particles or gives energy out when new attractions form.
Remember that first electron affinities release energy but second electron affinities need energy, so consider what that means for the sign overall.
walkthrough:
Sort processes into needing energy or releasing energy**
Think of it like pulling magnets apart versus letting them snap together. Pulling apart always needs energy put in, so $\Delta H$ is positive. Coming together releases energy, so $\Delta H$ is negative.

Apply this to atomisation, ionisation and lattice formation**
Atomisation is $\text{X(s)} \rightarrow \text{X(g)}$, breaking all bonds to give gaseous atoms. That always needs energy, so always positive. Ionisation is removing an electron from a gaseous atom against nuclear attraction, that always needs energy, so always positive. Lattice formation is gaseous ions coming together to form a solid lattice, $\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{g}) + 2\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2}(\text{s})$, new ionic bonds form, so energy is always released, always negative.

See why electron affinity is the odd one out**
First electron affinity, $\text{Cl(g)} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g})$, usually releases energy because the nucleus attracts the incoming electron. But second electron affinity, adding an electron to an already negative ion, needs energy to overcome repulsion. So electron affinity can be either positive or negative.

Final answer: electron affinity: either positive or negative
enthalpy change of atomisation: always positive
ionisation energy: always positive
lattice energy: always negative

hints: Identify what $\Delta H_{3}$ and $\Delta H_{4}$ represent on the cycle by looking at the species changing, $\text{Mg(g)}$ to $\text{Mg}^{+}(\text{g})$ and $\text{Mg}^{+}(\text{g})$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{g})$.
walkthrough:
Read the two steps from the diagram**
$\Delta H_{3}$ is $\text{Mg(g)} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{+}(\text{g}) + \text{e}^{-}$, the first ionisation. $\Delta H_{4}$ is $\text{Mg}^{+}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{g}) + \text{e}^{-}$, the second ionisation.

Compare the attraction felt by the electron**
In the second step you are pulling a negative electron away from a $1+$ ion to leave a $2+$ ion, rather than from a neutral atom. The higher positive charge pulls the remaining electrons in more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it. That is why $\Delta H_{4} > \Delta H_{3}$.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{4}$ is the second ionisation energy and $\Delta H_{3}$ is the first ionisation energy; the second electron is removed from a more positively charged ion so is held more strongly.

hints: Follow each arrow from start to finish: one arrow starts from gaseous ions and ends at the solid, the other starts from elements in standard states and ends at the solid.
walkthrough:
Match the arrow to the definition**
$\Delta H_{6}$ goes from $\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{g}) + 2\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g})$ down to $\text{MgCl}_{2}(\text{s})$. Gaseous ions forming one mole of solid lattice is exactly lattice energy.
$\Delta H_{7}$ goes from $\text{Mg(s)} + \text{Cl}_{2}(\text{g})$, the elements in their standard states, down to $\text{MgCl}_{2}(\text{s})$, one mole of compound. That is exactly the standard enthalpy change of formation.
Final answer: $\Delta H_{6}$ is lattice energy (enthalpy) and $\Delta H_{7}$ is (standard) enthalpy change of formation.

hints: Recall how atomic size and the distance of the outer shell from the nucleus change going down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine.
Link that distance to the strength of attraction between the nucleus and an incoming electron added to form a $1-$ ion.
walkthrough:
Picture what first electron affinity means**
It is $\text{X(g)} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{X}^{-}(\text{g})$. Energy is released when the nucleus pulls the incoming electron in. The stronger the pull, the more exothermic the value.

Track the size change down Group 17**
Going from $\text{F}$ to $\text{Cl}$ to $\text{Br}$ to $\text{I}$, a new electron shell is added each time. The outer shell gets further from the nucleus and there is more shielding by inner electrons, even though nuclear charge increases.

Connect distance to less energy released**
Because the incoming electron joins an orbital further away, the nucleus to electron distance is larger and the attraction is weaker. Less energy is released on forming the $1-$ ion, so electron affinity becomes less exothermic down the group.

Final answer: First electron affinity becomes less exothermic (less negative) down Group 17.
Down the group the atomic radius increases so the incoming electron is added further from the nucleus and experiences weaker nuclear attraction.

hints: Start with $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$ and check the moles of each substance in the equation carefully.
Remember the table value for $\text{O}_{2}$ is for one mole, but the equation uses $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}$, so you must halve it before substituting.

Recall $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and that $T$ must be in kelvin and $\Delta S$ must be converted from $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ to $\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ to match $\Delta H$.
Check the sign of your $\Delta S$ by thinking about moles of gas: gas is lost going to solid, so $\Delta S$ should be negative, and keep units for the final $\Delta G$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the entropy change**
Use:
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$$
For $\text{Mg(s)} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{MgO(s)}$:
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = S^{\ominus}(\text{MgO}) - [S^{\ominus}(\text{Mg}) + 0.5 \times S^{\ominus}(\text{O}_{2})]$$
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = 26.9 - (32.7 + 0.5 \times 205) = 26.9 - (32.7 + 102.5) = -108.3 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
The value is negative, which makes sense because $0.5$ mol of gas is converted into solid, so disorder decreases.

Set up Gibbs free energy with matching units**
Use:
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$
$T = 25^{\circ}\text{C} = 298 \text{ K}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus} = -602 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Convert $\Delta S$ to $\text{kJ}$: $-108.3 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = -0.1083 \text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Substitute and solve**
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -602 - (298 \times (-0.1083))$$
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -602 + 32.27 = -569.7 \approx -570 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
The large negative value shows the formation of $\text{MgO}$ is highly feasible at $298 \text{ K}$, driven by the very exothermic $\Delta H$ despite the unfavourable negative $\Delta S$.
